questions.problem:
Find the volume of the solid $R,$ given by

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,1\le y\le 3,\,0\le z\le 2y,\,0\le x\le y+2z}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that we have a three-dimensional type II region.

Therefore, the volume of $R$ is given by the following triple integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2y}{\int }_{0}^{y+2z}\,dx\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2y}[x]_{x=0}^{x=y+2z}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2y}y+2z\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}{[yz+{z}^{2}]}_{z=0}^{z=2y}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}y(2y)+(2y)^{2}-0\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}6{y}^{2}\,dy \\  & ={[2{y}^{3}]}_{y=1}^{y=3} \\  & =2(3)^{3}-2(1)^{3}-0 \\  & =52.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the volume of the solid $R$ given by

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,1\le y\le 4,\,2\le z\le 3y+x}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that we have a three-dimensional type I region.

Therefore, the volume of $R$ is given by the following triple integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{1}^{4}{\int }_{2}^{3y+x}\,dz\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{1}^{4}[z]_{z=2}^{z=3y+x}\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{1}^{4}3y+x-2\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{3}{2}{y}^{2}+xy-2y]}_{y=1}^{y=4}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\,[(24+4x-8)-(\frac{3}{2}+x-2)]\,dx \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2}3x+\frac{33}{2}\,dx \\  & ={[\frac{3{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{33}{2}x]}_{x=0}^{x=2} \\  & =\frac{3(2)^{2}}{2}+\frac{33}{2}(2)-0 \\  & =39.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the volume of the solid $R,$ given by

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,1\le z\le 3,\,0\le x\le 2z\operatorname{sin}⁡y}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that we have a three-dimensional type II region.

Therefore, the volume of $R$ is given by the following triple integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2z\operatorname{sin}⁡y}\,dx\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{1}^{3}[x]_{x=0}^{x=2z\operatorname{sin}⁡y}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{1}^{3}2z\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,{[{z}^{2}]}_{z=1}^{z=3}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y({3}^{2}-{1}^{2})\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}8\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,dy \\  & =8[-\operatorname{cos}⁡y]_{y=0}^{y=\pi /2} \\  & =-8(0-1) \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the volume of the solid region above.

*Hint: All surfaces, except for the top one, are parallel to the corresponding coordinate planes.*
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14064036/assets/66593acc794ee28d8372ec5758abf14594ea58528c1fe793917754dd9d21c5ad.png)

 

Notice that our solid can be written as the type I region

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,y)\in D,\,\,0\le z\le 6-3x-2y},
$$

where $D$ is the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane.

To find the top boundary curve of $D$ in the form $y=y(x),$ we substitute $z=0$ into the equation $z=6-3x-2y:$

$$
0=6-3x-2y\,⟹\,y=3-\frac{3}{2}x
$$

Then, we have

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,0\le y\le 3-\frac{3}{2}x},
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14064036/assets/8b3edbf61dc8a2b2a027c79a0ac1bbee54163b89277040119aaea382121998ff.png)

Hence, the type I representation of $R$ is

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,0\le y\le 3-\frac{3}{2}x,\,\,0\le z\le 6-3x-2y}.
$$

Therefore, the volume of $R$ is given by the following triple integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{3-3x/2}{\int }_{0}^{6-3x-2y}dz\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{3-3x/2}[z]_{z=0}^{z=6-3x-2y}\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{3-3x/2}(6-3x-2y)-0\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{3-3x/2}6-3x-2y\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[(6-3x)y-{y}^{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=3-3x/2}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}((6-3x)(3-\frac{3x}{2})-{(3-\frac{3x}{2})}^{2})-0\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(3-\frac{3x}{2})((6-3x)-(3-\frac{3x}{2}))\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(3-\frac{3x}{2})(3-\frac{3x}{2})\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{(3-\frac{3x}{2})}^{2}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}9-9x+\frac{9{x}^{2}}{4}\,dx \\  & ={[9x-\frac{9{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{3{x}^{3}}{4}]}_{x=0}^{x=2} \\  & =(9(2)-\frac{9(2)^{2}}{2}+\frac{3(2)^{3}}{4})-0 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that our solid can be written as the type III region

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,\,0\le y\le 4-2x-4z},
$$

where $D$ is the projection of $R$ onto the $xz$-plane.

To find the top boundary curve of $D$ in the form $z=z(x),$ we substitute $y=0$  into the equation $y=4-2x-4z:$

$$
0=4-2x-4z\,⟹\,z=1-\frac{x}{2}
$$

Then, we have

$$
D={(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,0\le z\le 1-\frac{x}{2}},
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14064036/assets/76fcca4251a904a08ac2f6ba8181d92c2c2fa7e07e596ef6276f1d21b574817a.png)

Hence, the type III representation of $R$ is

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,0\le z\le 1-\frac{x}{2},\,\,0\le y\le 4-2x-4z}.
$$

Therefore, the volume of $R$ is given by the following triple integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1-x/2}{\int }_{0}^{4-2x-4z}dy\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1-x/2}[y]_{y=0}^{y=4-2x-4z}\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1-x/2}(4-2x-4z)-0\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1-x/2}4-2x-4z\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[(4-2x)z-2{z}^{2}]}_{z=0}^{z=1-x/2}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}((4-2x)(1-\frac{x}{2})-2{(1-\frac{x}{2})}^{2})-0\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(1-\frac{x}{2})((4-2x)-2(1-\frac{x}{2}))\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{2}(2-x)(2-x)\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2-2x+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}\,dx \\  & ={[2x-{x}^{2}+\frac{{x}^{3}}{6}]}_{x=0}^{x=2} \\  & =(2(2)-{2}^{2}+\frac{{2}^{3}}{6})-0 \\  & =\frac{4}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the volume of the solid region enclosed by the planes $x=1-y$ and $x=y+1,$ and the planes $y=1,$ $y=2,$ $z=0,$ $z=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that our solid can be written as a type II region: 

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,1\le y\le 2,\,\,0\le z\le 1,\,\,1-y\le x\le y+1}
$$

Therefore, the volume of $R$ is given by the following triple integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1-y}^{y+1}\,dx\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}[x]_{x=1-y}^{x=y+1}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}y+1-(1-y)\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}2y\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}2y[z]_{z=0}^{z=1}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}2y\,dy \\  & =[{y}^{2}]_{y=1}^{y=2} \\  & ={2}^{2}-{1}^{2} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the volume of the solid region enclosed by the $xz$-plane and the surface $y=z{e}^{x},$ and the planes $x=-1,$ $x=0,$ $z=0,$ $z=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that our solid can be written as a type III region: 

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,-1\le x\le 0,\,\,0\le z\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le z{e}^{x}}
$$

Therefore, the volume of $R$ is given by the following triple integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{z{e}^{x}}dy\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{1}[y]_{y=0}^{y=z{e}^{x}}\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{1}z{e}^{x}\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{e}^{x}{[\frac{1}{2}{z}^{2}]}_{z=0}^{z=1}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}\frac{1}{2}{e}^{x}\,dx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[{e}^{x}]_{x=-1}^{x=0} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{0}-{e}^{-1}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(1-\frac{1}{e}) \\  & =\frac{e-1}{2e}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Double-Integral Formula for Volume
questions.problem:
Consider the solid enclosed between the paraboloid $x=-2+{y}^{2}+4{z}^{2}$ and the parabolic cylinder $x=-1+2{z}^{2},$ whose volume can be written in terms of double integrals, as follows:

$$
V={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{a(y)}^{b(y)}\,f(y,z)\,dz\,dy
$$

What is ${a}^{2}+{b}^{2}+f?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to determine the projection of the intersection of our surfaces onto the $yz$-plane. So, let's find where they intersect.

$$
\begin{aligned}-2+{y}^{2}+4{z}^{2} & =-1+2{z}^{2} \\ {y}^{2}+2{z}^{2} & =1 \\ {y}^{2}+2{z}^{2} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

So, the projection of the intersection in the $yz$-plane is an ellipse.

Notice that our solid can be written as a type II region: 

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,\,-2+{y}^{2}+4{z}^{2}\le x\le -1+2{z}^{2}},
$$

where $D$ is the interior of the ellipse ${y}^{2}+2{z}^{2}=1.$ 

As a result, the volume of $R$ is given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{-2+{y}^{2}+4{z}^{2}}^{-1+2{z}^{2}}\text{d}x]\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-1+2{z}^{2})-(-2+{y}^{2}+4{z}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}1-{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the boundary of $D$ consists of 

- the lower part $z=-\sqrt{\frac{1-{y}^{2}}{2}},$ and

- the upper part $z=\sqrt{\frac{1-{y}^{2}}{2}},$

for $-1\le y\le 1.$ 

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}1-{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-\sqrt{(1-{y}^{2})/2}}^{\sqrt{(1-{y}^{2})/2}}\,1-{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2}\,dz\,dy.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}+f & ={(-\sqrt{\frac{1-{y}^{2}}{2}})}^{2}+{(\sqrt{\frac{1-{y}^{2}}{2}})}^{2}+(1-{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1-{y}^{2}}{2}+\frac{1-{y}^{2}}{2}+(1-{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2}) \\  & =2-2{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Double-Integral Formula for Volume
questions.problem:
Consider the solid enclosed between the paraboloids $z=-3+6{x}^{2}+5{y}^{2}$ and $z=-1+5{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2},$ whose volume can be written in terms of double integrals, as follows:

$$
V={\int }_{-\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{2}}{\int }_{a(x)}^{b(x)}\,f(x,y)\,dy\,dx
$$

What is ${a}^{2}+{b}^{2}+f?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to determine the projection of the intersection of our surfaces onto the $xy$-plane. So, let's find where they intersect.

$$
\begin{aligned}-3+6{x}^{2}+5{y}^{2} & =-1+5{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2} \\ {x}^{2}+2{y}^{2} & =2\end{aligned}
$$

So, the projection of the intersection in the $xy$-plane is an ellipse.

Notice that our solid can be written as a type I region: 

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,y)\in D,\,\,-3+6{x}^{2}+5{y}^{2}\le z\le -1+5{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}},
$$

where $D$ is the interior of the ellipse ${x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}=2.$ 

As a result, the volume of $R$ is given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{-3+6{x}^{2}+5{y}^{2}}^{-1+5{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}}\text{d}z]\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-1+5{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2})-(-3+6{x}^{2}+5{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2-{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the boundary of $D$ consists of

- the lower part $y=-\sqrt{1-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}},$ and

- the upper part $y=\sqrt{1-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}},$

for $-\sqrt{2}\le x\le \sqrt{2}.$ 

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2-{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{-\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{2}}{\int }_{-\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}/2}}^{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}/2}}\,2-{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}\,dy\,dx.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}+f & ={(-\sqrt{1-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}})}^{2}+{(\sqrt{1-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}})}^{2}+(2-{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}) \\  & =1-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+1-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+(2-{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}) \\  & =4-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Double-Integral Formula for Volume
questions.problem:
Consider the solid enclosed between the parabolic cylinders $y=4{x}^{2}$ and $y=1-2{z}^{2},$ whose volume can be written in terms of double integrals, as follows:

$$
V={\int }_{-1/2}^{1/2}{\int }_{a(x)}^{b(x)}\,f(x,z)\,dz\,dx
$$

What is ${a}^{2}+{b}^{2}+f?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to determine the projection of the intersection of our surfaces onto the $xz$-plane. So, let's find where they intersect.

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2} & =1-2{z}^{2} \\ 4{x}^{2}+2{z}^{2} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

So, the projection of the intersection in the $xz$-plane is an ellipse.

Notice that our solid can be written as a type III region: 

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,\,4{x}^{2}\le y\le 1-2{z}^{2}},
$$

where $D$ is the interior of the elipse $4{x}^{2}+2{z}^{2}=1.$ 

As a result, the volume of $R$ is given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{4{x}^{2}}^{1-2{z}^{2}}\text{d}y]\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(1-2{z}^{2})-(4{x}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}1-2{z}^{2}-4{x}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the boundary of $D$ consists of 

- the lower part $z=-\sqrt{\frac{1-4{x}^{2}}{2}},$ and

- the upper part $z=\sqrt{\frac{1-4{x}^{2}}{2}},$

for $-\frac{1}{2}\le x\le \frac{1}{2}.$ 

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}1-2{z}^{2}-4{x}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{-1/2}^{1/2}{\int }_{-\sqrt{(1-4{x}^{2})/2}}^{\sqrt{(1-4{x}^{2})/2}}\,1-2{z}^{2}-4{x}^{2}\,dz\,dx.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}+f & ={(-\sqrt{\frac{1-4{x}^{2}}{2}})}^{2}+{(\sqrt{\frac{1-4{x}^{2}}{2}})}^{2}+(1-2{z}^{2}-4{x}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1-4{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{1-4{x}^{2}}{2}+(1-2{z}^{2}-4{x}^{2}) \\  & =2-8{x}^{2}-2{z}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Double-Integral Formula for Volume
questions.problem:
Consider the solid enclosed between the paraboloid $x=3{y}^{2}+4{z}^{2}$ and the parabolic cylinder $x=1-{y}^{2},$ whose volume can be written in terms of double integrals, as follows:

$$
V={\int }_{-1/2}^{1/2}{\int }_{a(y)}^{b(y)}\,f(y,z)\,dz\,dy
$$

What is ${a}^{2}+{b}^{2}+f?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to determine the projection of the intersection of our surfaces onto the $yz$-plane. So, let's find where they intersect.

$$
\begin{aligned}3{y}^{2}+4{z}^{2} & =1-{y}^{2} \\ 4{y}^{2}+4{z}^{2} & =1 \\ {y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the projection of the intersection in the $yz$-plane is a circle.

Notice that our solid can be written as a type II region: 

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,\,3{y}^{2}+4{z}^{2}\le x\le 1-{y}^{2}},
$$

where $D$ is the interior of the circle ${y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=\frac{1}{4}.$ 

As a result, the volume of $R$ is given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{3{y}^{2}+4{z}^{2}}^{1-{y}^{2}}\text{d}x]\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(1-{y}^{2})-(3{y}^{2}+4{z}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}1-4{y}^{2}-4{z}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the boundary of $D$ consists of 

- the lower part $z=-\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{1-4{y}^{2}},$ and

- the upper part $z=\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{1-4{y}^{2}},$

for $-\frac{1}{2}\le y\le \frac{1}{2}.$ 

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}1-4{y}^{2}-4{z}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{-1/2}^{1/2}{\int }_{-\sqrt{1-4{y}^{2}}/2}^{\sqrt{1-4{y}^{2}}/2}\,1-4{y}^{2}-4{z}^{2}\,dz\,dy.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}+f & ={(-\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{1-4{y}^{2}})}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{1-4{y}^{2}})}^{2}+(1-4{y}^{2}-4{z}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(1-4{y}^{2})+\frac{1}{4}(1-4{y}^{2})+(1-4{y}^{2}-4{z}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}-6{y}^{2}-4{z}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Double-Integral Formula for Volume
questions.problem:
Consider the solid enclosed between the parabolic cylinders $y=-2+3{x}^{2}$ and $y=-4{z}^{2},$ whose volume can be written in terms of double integrals, as follows:

$$
V={\int }_{-\sqrt{6}/3}^{\sqrt{6}/3}{\int }_{a(x)}^{b(x)}\,f(x,z)\,dz\,dx
$$

What is ${a}^{2}+{b}^{2}+f?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to determine the projection of the intersection of our surfaces onto the $xz$-plane. So, let's find where they intersect.

$$
\begin{aligned}-2+3{x}^{2} & =-4{z}^{2} \\ 3{x}^{2}+4{z}^{2} & =2\end{aligned}
$$

So, the projection of the intersection in the $xz$-plane is an ellipse.

Notice that our solid can be written as a type III region: 

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,\,-2+3{x}^{2}\le y\le -4{z}^{2}},
$$

where $D$ is the interior of the ellipse $3{x}^{2}+4{z}^{2}=2.$ 

As a result, the volume of $R$ is given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{-2+3{x}^{2}}^{-4{z}^{2}}\text{d}y]\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-4{z}^{2})-(-2+3{x}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2-3{x}^{2}-4{z}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the boundary of $D$ consists of 

- the lower part $z=-\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{2-3{x}^{2}},$ and

- the upper part $z=\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{2-3{x}^{2}},$

for $-\frac{\sqrt{6}}{3}\le x\le \frac{\sqrt{6}}{3}.$ 

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2-3{x}^{2}-4{z}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{-\sqrt{6}/3}^{\sqrt{6}/3}{\int }_{-\sqrt{2-3{x}^{2}}/2}^{\sqrt{2-3{x}^{2}}/2}\,2-3{x}^{2}-4{z}^{2}\,dz\,dx.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}+f & ={(-\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{2-3{x}^{2}})}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{2-3{x}^{2}})}^{2}+(2-3{x}^{2}-4{z}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{2-3{x}^{2}}{4}+\frac{2-3{x}^{2}}{4}+(2-3{x}^{2}-4{z}^{2}) \\  & =3-\frac{9}{2}{x}^{2}-4{z}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Volume of a Solid Given in Set Notation
canonical_examples.problem:
Find the volume of the solid $R,$ given by

$$
R = \Big\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: 1 \leq y \leq 2, \: 0 \leq z \leq \sqrt{2y}, \: 0 \leq x \leq yz \Big\}.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Notice that we have a three-dimensional type II region.

Therefore, the volume of $R$ is given by the following triple integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2y}}{\int }_{0}^{yz}\,dx\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2y}}[x]_{x=0}^{x=yz}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2y}}yz\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}y{[\frac{{z}^{2}}{2}]}_{z=0}^{z=\sqrt{2y}}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{y}{2}{(\sqrt{2y})}^{2}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{y}^{2}\,dy \\  & ={[\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{y=1}^{y=2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(8-1)-0 \\  & =\frac{7}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that our solid can be written as the type I region

$$
R = \big\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: (x,y) \in D, \:\: 0 \leq z \leq 4-x-y \big\},
$$

where

$$
D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \:\: 0 \leq y \leq 2 \big\}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane, shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14064036/assets/e19ffe6a0555851c2b05526272beb21dbcdc082a23a2e11809c661666efdf133.png)

Hence, the type I representation of $R$ is

$$
R = \big\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \:\: 0 \leq y \leq 2, \:\: 0 \leq z \leq 4-x-y \big\}.
$$

Therefore, the volume of $R$ is given by the following triple integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{4-x-y}dz\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}[z]_{z=0}^{z=4-x-y}\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}(4-x-y)-0\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}4-x-y\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[(4-x)y-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=2}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}((4-x)(2)-\frac{{2}^{2}}{2})-0\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}6-2x\,dx \\  & =[6x-{x}^{2}]_{x=0}^{x=1} \\  & =(6(1)-{1}^{2})-0 \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$
